items.title: Your "don't freeze into doctrine"
items.where: We Want Freedom Inside & Out!, P3
items.my_version: The motto would be: “Nothing suppressed, everything processed.” Each of us guides our own compatible practice, and our practices weave the community into the quilt that keeps us all warm and safe. Whatever answers we find stay fluid and organic, and don’t freeze into doctrine.

items.title: A practice group already is community
items.where: Practicing Community Can Start Now, P3
items.my_version: People sometimes buy forty acres and then bring all their unprocessed stuff with them to a more scenic location. It’s a more beautiful view for sure, but now you have the conflict PLUS goats. A group that practices together weekly for two years may never own land. So what? It’s already a real piece of community, and it can still make a difference when people are going through a divorce, an illness or grief. Parenting too, and plain old loneliness.

items.title: Quote marks Emulate put around three words
items.my_version:
Then there are the people who aren’t fully in the commune politically. Visitors, volunteers, workers, renters and interns at the commune (yes, even interns) are entitled to some rights when decisions really affect their pay or access to common resources. All of them should have clear terms, and the chance to be heard and to have such decisions reviewed. The same is true for decisions really affecting their schedule, safety, housing, records or discipline. Equality that stops at the membership line can end up recreating a servant class that moves from commune to commune.

Sénégal is unlike anywhere else I’ve lived. It’s the only Sufi Muslim country (aside from Gambia, a tiny nation inside Sénégal). Sufi muslims are the ones who value a deep, personal connection with God, rather than just following the religious rules. Five times a day the prayers pour out into the streets. I find them so soothing. And Sufism doesn’t stay inside designated spiritual places here. It’s in the music, in the pictures everywhere, in the murals, in the names, in the conversations. Prostitution is also legal here.

Solidarity doesn’t mean every community is liable for whatever the others owe, and it doesn’t mean anyone has an unlimited claim on another community’s labor and stores, or its land and tools. Even if nobody uses money internally, communities still need the same honesty about exchanges and obligations. Decide in advance which offers of help are purely goodwill and which go on a ledger of mutual aid. The federation can keep track of these for each purpose, without having to put a value on them or require every exchange to be even.

items.title: Who steps aside, and the appeal
items.where: When Somebody Has to Go, P2
items.my_version: This power to remove people is so easily abused, though. So work out the process before it’s about anyone in particular. What counts as cause for immediate protective action? Who has to step aside because they’re too close to it? Who decides to put temporary restrictions on someone? Who will make sure all the evidence is preserved? How will the person be able to reply to the concerns? What review or appeal is possible without endangering others? What protections will there be for the person’s interests (housing, records, family contact, access to common resources, outside funds if any) during the separation? When is it time to bring in outside help?

items.title: Autonomy doesn't erase rights
items.where: When Somebody Has to Go, P3
items.my_version: Note that “outside” doesn’t have to mean the nation-state. My research initially leaned too far that way. The basic need here is for a competent level of authority that is not reviewing its own conduct. That could mean another community, a federation of communities, professionals, autonomous regional institutions, courts, regulatory agencies, emergency services, etc. The key is that it’s not the same people. And a community’s autonomy doesn’t let it take away rights a person can’t sign away, or make the law outside disappear.
